items.title: Show HN: Lettercamp – open-source static blog framework
items.summary: Hi HN, I’m Eric and I’m building Lettercamp, an open-source static blog framework. The repo is at https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and the homepage is online at https://www.lettercamp.com . Writing good content has always been the #1 way that I’ve grown the reach of products I’ve worked on in the past. However, it’s always bothered me how many little things get in the way of writing and publishing high quality, first party content onto the web. Building a performant, SEO-optimized blog from scratch was always distracting from development on the actual product, and setting up a 3rd party CMS meant that my content always lived in someone else’s database. Storing content in a non-markdown format also made it difficult to draft and edit with the help of an AI agent. Lettercamp is a modern approach to creating a content site. It ships with all the little features you’d expect in a blog: pagination, authors, metadata, search, cross linking, related posts and more. It’s also statically built, which means that all your content lives in markdown in your codebase, so a deployed version is performant with no database to maintain. This means that you can focus on writing good content instead of vibe-coding a whole blog. I want to add more features to the framework over time, including better support for AI agents, built in localization, email sign ups, and more. The repo is released under the MIT license so that anyone can use the framework to create a content site. The goal isn’t to charge individual developers. The monetization path is to provide a cloud hosted version, that has an online editor that content teams can use. The main advantage of this is to decouple the blog from product deploys, so that teams can publish content without needing to push code. I would love to get your feedback on if this is a problem that might resonate with you or your team. I know that a lot of products create a /blog section at some point, and I wonder what solutions people are using today. My hope is that over time, Lettercamp can be the go-to solution for teams looking to set this up. Try it out: https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and let me know what you think!

items.title: Show HN: Spared – self-hosted Workers and Durable Objects for Rust apps
items.summary: Hi HN, I wanted something like workerd + celld for untrusted Rust apps and couldn’t find anything that quite fit. That said, I got a lot of inspiration from workerd, celld, spin, and wasmcloud. spared (spare-dee) runs Rust apps + SQLite in isolated WASM sandboxes. It lets you run many apps per server, and by packaging SQLite inside the sandbox, you get better isolation than running it on the host. This opens the door to running untrusted code on a single machine. It's open source and runs on any VPS. It's still early, and there's still a lot to build, but it feels like it's at a good place to share. Let me know what you think. Repo: https://github.com/michaelmagan/spared

items.title: Show HN: Rebuilding Amazon SES in Rust
items.summary: I'm Kam, co-founder and CTO of Nitrosend. Email is our lifeblood, so we've been gradually moving our email sending onto bare-metal servers and IPs we control. We wanted to make that move without rewriting the application code already calling Amazon SES. So we built NitroMTA, an open-source SES replacement in Rust. We kept our existing SES v2 sending calls and changed the endpoint and credentials to send through our own engine. We've been running it in production for a few weeks, moving more mail over as we warm our IPs and build reputation with each mailbox provider. Keep the SES integration For an application using boto3, this is the client configuration: import boto3 ses = boto3.client( "sesv2", region_name="us-east-1", endpoint_url="https://mail.example.com", ) For the SES v2 sending operations we support, the existing calls keep working. We test the official JavaScript, Python and Ruby SDKs against the engine, along with Nodemailer and django-ses. The compatibility page lists the operations and differences from SES: https://nitromta.com/docs/compatibility/ Measuring against KumoMTA and Postfix In our published 2 November comparison, NitroMTA sustained 3.16 times KumoMTA's throughput and 4.11 times Postfix's. These numbers measure SMTP submission and delivery. Engine Messages per second NitroMTA 3,313 KumoMTA 1,048 Postfix with OpenDKIM 806 Each engine had four CPU cores and 2 GiB of memory on the same AWS c7gd.metal bare-metal server, with its queue on local NVMe. The workload used 16 KiB messages, authenticated SMTP submission, TLS on submission and delivery, and RSA-2048 DKIM signing. Every engine committed a message to disk before acknowledging it. The figures are medians of three interleaved runs per engine. The quick profile searches for the highest rate meeting its latency budgets using ten-second load steps, delivering to one receiver site with no added network delay. Across the nine runs, the harness sent 1.35 million messages and checked that each arrived once, with its body intact and its DKIM signature valid. KumoMTA used its RocksDB spool with set_force_sync(true) to meet the same acceptance contract. KumoMTA documents that this forces database-wide flushes and can substantially reduce performance. The comparison is for that synchronous-acceptance contract; the harness also supports measuring its default asynchronous mode separately. The method, configurations, exact versions and raw results are published, and you can run the comparison with cargo harness quick: https://nitromta.com/docs/benchmarks/ Give each IP a budget for each provider An IP needs a sending history with the receivers it sends to. We need to decide how much volume it gets today, what earns it more tomorrow, and what makes us back off. We track the budget by sending IP and receiver group. That lets us hold an IP's Gmail cap while increasing its cap elsewhere, or lower its Outlook.com cap when Microsoft's responses call for it. With warmup enabled, the shipped ladder starts at 50 messages a day. A day needs enough SMTP outcomes to test its cap before it earns an increase. Complaints, failures, deferrals and throttling can hold the cap or move it down a rung. The Outlook.com defaults take fourteen clean daily increases to reach 10,000 messages a day. The default ladder takes seven. Both are configurable. Before any of this, the host needs outbound port 25 and reverse DNS control for its sending addresses. The domains need SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and bounce and complaint reports need somewhere to arrive. We put the setup checks in nitromta doctor, which prints the missing records. Provider feedback and durability details continue in a reply.

items.title: Show HN: Dedoomify – AI news, minus the doom
items.summary: What if AI failures were described like ordinary software issues? Paste a link to an AI article and dedoomify turns down the apocalypse: "the model is misaligned" becomes "the model has a bug". Less Skynet. More software. And every change is highlighted with the original text one hover or tap away. You can try an example without signing up or installing anything! The default engine runs on quick phrase rules or you can run a local AI model in your browser via WebGPU; there's also a Chrome extension that applies the rules to the page you’re reading. And all the code is open source! https://github.com/akspad/dedoomify There's so much AI doom in the world right now that I wanted to see what articles would look like reframed to be less doom and gloom and instead more matter-of-fact (sprinkled with some sunshine and roses). Let me know what you think - suggestions and improvements are always welcome :)
